Presidential Ramblings
By Steve Hansen
My introduction to John Jordan was in 1999 at the
Tacoma AAW Symposium where he and David Ellsworth ran a discussion entitled “How to Demonstrate”. The one thing I remember from their engaging “demo” was, as John stated, if you make a
mistake during a presentation (catch, projectile,
etc.) don’t be flustered - just carry on the demo –
mistakes happen. Take that opportunity to explain
why you made that mistake. Your audience will
respect you for it. John’s astounding body of work
is underlined by, among other factors, his deliberate approach to every cut, every detail, and every
textured dimple – it’s all done by hand, one at a
time. He never seemed to leave anything by
chance. As a founding member of the AAW and a
long-time advisor to the AAW he leaves us with an
incredible legacy that we all benefit from.
John Hammond gave us a great talk on Celtic Knot
design. For years I have wondered how these complex, intertwined figures could be laid out. My eureka moment came when John drew a freehand
closed squiggly onto the whiteboard and proceeded to show the process on rendering that wondering line into a over and under knot form – fantastic!
The President’s Challenge for April is “sphere” – try
your hand at making a sphere without the aid of a
jig. For bonus points try making several and show
them to the gallery from the first to latest
attempts.
Steve

Editor’s Notes
By Steve Fairbairn
We open our newsletter this month with a memoriam to John Jordan by Art Liestman. Next is the
regular monthly recap of the February TechTalk
session. This month’s Member Profile features
long time member, Allan Cusworth.
Sheila has provided us with some useful information about health at the lathe with a link to an
excellent AAW/WIT video on the topic as well as
the latest Women In Turning updates.
I’m happy to be able to reprint Part One of a Chainsaw Safety Seminar, delivered in 2023 by Al
Lundgren, to the Comox Valley Woodturners Society and is reprinted with his permission. Part Two:
Bar and Chain Maintenance will appear in the April
2023 newsletter and Part Three: History of the
Chain Saw will appear in the May 2023 newsletter.
As usual, I’m always soliciting articles on any
woodturning or guild related topics or tips. I’m also
hoping to be able to include a regular safety article
or tip in the newsletter and am looking for a member who is willing to take on that role.
Steve

In Memoriam - John Jordan
By Art Liestman
The woodturning world lost one of the greats
when John Jordan passed away on Feb. 28, 2023
(his 73rd birthday).
John was turning wood as a high school student in
1967 and became a professional woodturner at a
time when such creatures were few and far between. John was one of the founders of the AAW
and was instrumental in the association’s goal of
openly sharing ideas, methods and techniques,
and learning by example. He was made a Lifetime
AAW Honorary Member in 2012 and was one of
only two members who had attended every one
of the 36 AAW International Woodturning Symposiums to date.
His work (primarily turned and carved vessels) is
in numerous private and corporate collections
(Continued on page 5)

March 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page
5
(including the White House Collection) and in the
collections of over 30 museums (including the
Smithsonian). In addition to having easily recognizable signature work, he was open to exploring
other items such as teapots.
John was also a tool maker (making excellent hollowing tools and a great double ended shear
scraper). He did the metal work to make these
tools himself in a metal shop adjacent to his
woodturning studio. He also sold other tools and
lathes and was often a vendor at major symposia.
Many of us learned a great deal from John
through his videos, live demos, and classes. His
first videos were on VHS - one on bowl turning
and one on hollow turning. More recently he released a 2 dvd set on The Aesthetics and Properties of Wood. He also wrote a book on
Woodturning and published articles in the American Woodturner. We were fortunate enough to
have John as a demonstrator and teacher at the
first GVWG West Coast Roundup symposium in
2007. He returned in 2011 to do a full day demo
for the club and teach classes. Most recently he
did an online demo for us in 2021.
I will remember John for a great many things that
he taught me and for his friendship. I was one of
those who learned a lot from his videos. Back in
those (VHS) days, my wife Jan would generally
leave the room whenever I watched woodturning
videos but, when John’s videos were on, she stuck
around. She really enjoyed John’s Tennessee accent and folksy sayings - he was charming!
John and his wife Vicki lived in a heritage home
outside of Nashville - an old farm house that has
been in Vicki’s family for many generations. It’s
the sort of place that had a detached building for
the kitchen.
In 2013, I stayed with John and Vicki for several
days. On the first day, they took me to the Frist
Museum in Nashville to see an exhibit called Sensuous Steel (I recommend googling for images of
that show). I was a bit reluctant to go as I was
very tired, and the exhibit was about cars which
generally don’t interest me. However, this exhibit
was spectacular, featuring rare Art Deco era cars
and motorcycles. These objects were stunning.
They had amazing curves that seemed to change
as you walked around them and were painted
with spectacular colours! I’ve spent a few times
with woodturners that completely changed my
view of things, and this museum visit was one of
them. I still have little interest in cars, but I
learned a lot about curves that day. John knew
that this exhibit would change my way of seeing
things and make an impact on my own work.
John stayed at my house a few times when he
was in Vancouver and Jan and I visited the Jordans when we were in Nashville in 2017. On that
trip, we attended the recording of a live radio
concert, ate some great food, went to a botanical
garden, and generally touristed around.
John received a liver transplant in 2020 and was
on immunosuppressant drugs. Unfortunately,
early this year he developed a fungus in his lungs
which is life threatening to immunocompromised
patients. He spent his last week or so fighting this
in the hospital but succumbed on Feb. 28. He is
greatly missed by his family and all who knew
him.
To end on a more upbeat note: In an artist statement for a show held in 2001, John submitted images of rocks and bark that he found inspiring and
said “…Surfaces and textures, patterns, and repetitions, both natural and man-made, landscapes
and architecture, contemporary as well as ancient
and ethnic objects interest me greatly. The effects
of music, of all sorts, and a comfortable, relaxing
place to work certainly have an impact on what I
produce. My emotional and physical states as well
enter into my work. But, without question, the
strongest and most direct influence and source of
inspiration I have is – the work that I am making.
The second strongest influence or source of inspiration is the material that I use.”
(Continued from page 4)

Tech Talk
By Bruce Campbell
Our regularly schedules Tech Talk ZOOM session of
2023 as held at 7:00PM on Monday February 27th
– the Monday after our Guild meeting. We had
about 30 attendees and, as usual, the discussion
was wide-ranging and informative.
Our members are really imaginative in their questions and advice as well as in their contributions.
One submission was truly exceptional this month.
So much so that I have elected NOT to write it up
here in hopes that the contributor will take steps
to commercialize the idea. I also would like to ask
all those that attended the session to keep the idea
private. Just remember Fraser, most of us on the
call want one from the first commercial batch.
Making a Shop Bench
Sheila started us off last time by asking for our
thoughts on converting a dresser drawer set into a
workbench on wheels. She has a small shop so
wants a workbench on wheels and her shop floor is
smooth. The dresser drawer in question would be
“free” for her. Here is a picture:
I began with two observations regarding the drawers. The first is that they typically rest on the
frame of the dresser rather than being on slides.
This would make them hard to open if they had any
significant weight in them. Second, dresser drawers usually do not have heavy bottoms in them so,
again, they would not handle much weight.
Another participant mentioned that a usual dresser
drawer set does not have a very solid back; often
thin plywood tacked in place. This would make the
unit unsteady.
Further discussion revealed that Sheila would like a
vise on the bench and that lead to a discussion on
how to reinforce the top to accommodate both the
weight and the implied stress on the frame.
Another person pointed out that it would be difficult to get in close to the bench unless it was raised
to make room for feet.
In the end we decided that it would likely be easier
and more cost effective to design and build a
bench from scratch. Sometimes “free” is just too
expensive.
Thanks for the question, Sheila.
Gouge Feels A Little Small
Scott commented that his newly purchased 5/8”
RG Wood gouge fells a bit small and he feels like he
is getting more vibration than he expected.
This prompted some discussion about the reasons
why this might be but little was resolved.
Dan, who also own one of these tools as well as
other 5/8” gouges, took the time to measure them
and reported that the RG Wood tool is made from
15mm round stock while competitors measure
(Continued on page 7)
Tech Talk is held on the Monday evening following
the Guild ZOOM session. The credentials for the
session are sent to all registered Guild members
and all are encouraged to participate in the freeflowing discussion centered on technical aspects of
woodturning.
Dresser for workbench conversion

16mm. This is likely to do with metric vs Imperial
“standards”.
Scott must have been turning a lot lately to “feel”
that difference.
Purchasing a Beading and Parting Tool
Diana asked on advice on which beading and
parting tool to buy; a 3/8” or a 1/2". If she were
planning on using it as a beading tool then I would
advise she choose the one closer to the size of
bead she would most commonly be turning. While
both than be used on any sized bead on that is
closer to the size of the bead being cut is easier to
use. If it is intended to be used mostly as a wide
parting tool then I would suggest the 3/8” size as it
will be easier to control.
Another way to decide is to visit a member near
you and try theirs.
Preserving OSMOE Finish
Gwenda finds that her remaining OSMOE waterbased finish is skinning over in the can and asked
what could be used to prevent that. In addition,
she asked if anyone had used a thinner for it.
On the issue of skinning over, we had a fairly
lengthy discussion on the topic during our November 2022 Tech Talk. Have a look at page 5 here:
https://gvwg.ca/docs/Newsletter2023/
January2023.pdf
As for thinning, Gary reports that he has used acetone as a thinner with success and feels it goes on
a little easier. Additional discussion suggested that
temperature – especially cold - can play a big part
in how the product performs. My shop is unheated
so gets very cold in winter. As a result, I store my
water-based finishes and glues inside.
Epoxy Handling Hack
Brian came up with a great hack to make it easier
to manage his epoxy glue. He buys the large
bottles but finds them clumsy to use. So, he pur-

chased and inexpensive pair of 60CC syringes from
a farm supply company, removed the plunger,
filled one with resin and the other with hardener
and re-inserted the plungers. Then he was able to
find plastic caps that fit over the syringe nozzles
and being a wood turner made wooden caps to

EMTECH on Pens
Bill turns a lot of pens and has been experimenting
with various finishes. He reports that EMTECH
gives him a great finish but does not last. His test
pen began to dull within a month of regular use.
Knowing Bill, he will keep looking but meanwhile
he is sticking with CA glue as a pen finish.
Many thanks to all that took part last time and I
hope the see more of you at our next session
scheduled for Monday, March 27th at 7:00 PM
over ZOOM. Watch your email for an invitation
including the ZOOM credentials.
Until then, I wish you safe and happy turning.

This Month’s Cover - ”Hot Tea”
By Larry Stevenson
I decided to use an existing dry form and work
from there.
I selected a dry roughed out maple form and then
decided to use existing forms that I normally turn
to enhance it.
This led to designing the lid and the finial to resemble the tops I make for urns.
The handle is burled maple to give grain strength
and the spout is just plain maple.
Dimensions are 6.5" height , pot is 4.5" diameter
not including spout and handle.
Finish is acrylics with texture of Kroma Crackle.
The texture is known as Demented Derma.
Look up videos on this technique
Dry brushed acrylics to emulate ash on burning
wood and the protective coating is Emtech Water
based Lacquer (satin).

Tell us about your background - how did you
get into woodturning?
When we were kids at home, my brother and I
made toy wagons, bulldozers, and anything we
could imagine out of the scraps of wood that my
dad had around home. That’s where my love of
working with wood started. You might say that it
was “ingrained” in me at an early age!
I went to high school at Cobourg District Collegiate
Institute in Cobourg, Ontario. My home room in
Grade 10 was the Industrial Arts Shop; my teacher
was Mr. Henry Morrison. In my opinion, he was
way ahead of his time. His infamous statement,
“the project is not finished until the floor is swept”
stays with me to this day. I think of him every time
I sweep up my shavings. It was there that I first saw
a woodturning lathe. I can’t remember what I
made but it must have shaped me into being a
woodturner later in life.
In the mid-60’s I met my lifelong partner, Natalia, a
Portuguese girl from the Azores, in Little Current,
Northern Ontario during a six-month work project
there. Two years later, we got married and set up
our home in Cobourg.
(Continued on page 10)
Guild Member Profile - Allan Cusworth
By Allan Cusworth

March 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page
10
I changed from a construction clerical career to
Purchasing around the same time. While visiting an
Industrial Supplies vendor in town I noticed they
had a Rockwell Beaver gap bed wood lathe with
motor for sale for $189.00. That was a lot of money
in those days. Since our home had a basement
where I could set up a shop, I bought it.
Since it had been quite few years since I was in Mr.
Morrison’s class, I decided to take a night school
session to refresh my woodturning skills. Mr. Morrison had long since retired and the new teacher
was quite dismayed when I told him I wanted to
make a bowling pin shaped lamp with strips of contrasting wood colours. I wanted the large diameter
sections to be wide and as the neck narrowed, I
wanted the colour of the strip to narrow too. He
said he would think about it and get back to me the
next week.
Meanwhile Natalia and I were having supper one
evening and she was about to cut an apple pie. It
struck me! If we were looking at the top of my
lamp, and each piece of the pie was a different colour the strips of colour wood narrow as it was being shaped.
I took this revelation to my next class and told the
teacher. He had spent a lot of time with a protractor and ruler trying to calculate the angles we
would need to set the table saw at to cut the pieces. He was a little dismayed that he had not figured
the easy way out; just count the number of pieces
on pie and divide that number into 360 degrees.
Here’s a picture of that lamp.
I was employes in a Purchasing position in Sarnia,
Ontario from 1989 till 1994. I did some woodturning there but did not take it seriously. In 1994, I
was offered a Purchasing Manager’s job in Vancouver, BC, so Natalia and I packed up everything, including my Rockwell Beaver lathe and moved to
British Columbia.
Our first house in Surrey did not have a basement
so the Beaver lathe staying in the garage getting
rusty. It wasn’t until 1999 when we built a house in
Fraser Heights in Surrey that I set up a shop, removed the rust, and started turning again. Here’s
where I started getting serious about the craft. I
was shopping for some finish for a piece I was making, and I met Bill Olsen at Windsor Plywood in
Fleetwood. He quizzed me on what I was doing and
asked me if I was interested in going to a
Woodturners Guild meeting with he and a couple
of other guys, namely Colin Delory, and Garry
Cormier. I accepted his invitation, since he had given me a 10% discount on the container of finish I
bought that day.
I was working in Delta at the time, so I rushed over
to Bill’s place in Surrey, and he took me to a Fraser
Valley Woodturners Guild meeting in Abbotsford. I
was impressed with welcoming and friendliness of
the turners there. Shortly thereafter, he invited me
to go to New Westminster to a Greater Vancouver
Woodturners Guild meeting. That’s where I met
some people who are friends today.
(Continued from page 9)
(Continued on page 11)

March 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page
11
Tell us about your workshop/studio.
At my workshop in Fraser Heights, I practiced the
techniques that I learned at both Guilds. It was
Woodturning 101 with Gerry Vickers, the Saturday
demonstrations that brought in world class turners,
the three GVWG West Coast Round-Up Symposiums that I helped with, and the countless one-onone sessions with the masters at the Guilds that
gave me the tools to hone my turning skills to
make this hobby so much fun.
I had a short stint with the Craftsman lathe you see
in the next picture, but it was a real “dog”, and I
returned it to Sears and went back to turning on
my Beaver lathe. I outfitted that shop with my first
bandsaw, drill press and jointer. Now I could cut
my own blanks and that expanded my abilities.
That was fun.
After a few years and some work-related health
challenges, Natalia and I moved to our present
home in Langley. I converted the bedroom of the
basement suite into my woodturning studio and
moved my machinery in. Thanks to Bill Olsen and
Colin Delory for making that move a lot easier.
I sold my Beaver lathe and upgraded to a Nova
DVRxp machine shortly thereafter.
What tools do you like using at your lathe?
Like most turners, I found out that a lathe is the
cheapest part of this hobby as I started to invest
further into quality tools. Quality tools lead to quality pieces. I like to use the best tool available for
each task at hand. I rough down spindles with a
Spindle Roughing Gouge; I turn bowls with a Bowl
Gouge, and so on. I really do like using my skew to
get a real smooth surface without a lot of sanding.
What is your favourite wood?
I have two woods that I prefer to turn. The first is
West Coast Big Leaf Maple. It’s not only a local species but it is also a beautiful wood to work with. I
make my Wedding Goblets mostly from BL Maple.
The other wood I really like is Red Alder with its
beautiful medullar ray configurations. I do use
some exotic woods for finials and other special
pieces.
What finishes do you prefer using?
For my Salad Bowls, candy dishes and other small
bowls, I use Danish Oil. It is considered food safe
after it dries completely and is very easy to apply
even off the lathe. For other small items, like Bottle
stoppers and handles, I like to use Shellawax
Cream. I also like using wipe-on Polyurethane for a
glossy finish on some vessels.
I guess the piece I am most known for is my Wedding Goblet with captive stem rings. I have done
quite a few demonstrations of the method I use to
make them and really like turning them out of Big
Leaf Maple. I have made close to 200 of them over
the years.
(Continued from page 10)
(Continued on page 12)

I have tried my hand at making a lot of other pieces
some of which include Christmas ornaments, Tulips
and Daffodils, and Pepper Mills.
One of the most rewarding things I have been involved with while being a member of the GVWG is
the time spent editing the Newsletter with the late
Barry Wilkinson as the publisher. We worked very
(Continued from page 11)

closely together to make the publication the best
we could. Barry designed the newsletter format
and passed it on to the next publisher. That format
was used until the last couple of years. We entered
Barry’s format into the American Association on
Woodturners annual Best Newsletter competition
and were tied for second place in 2008. The AAW
awarded us third place after they drew lots to decide on the second and third place categories.
Other pursuits
Writing Articles - Quite a few years ago at the Cloverdale Wood Show, the editor of Canadian Woodworking and Home Improvement magazine saw
one of my wedding goblets on display and asked
me if I would be willing to write an article on how I
made it for their magazine. I consented to do so
and have now written fourteen articles on different
woodturning projects. My most recent one was
published in their December 2022/January 2023
issue called, “Turning a Tulip.” I have offered an inperson demonstration to the GVWG of this process
and would welcome the opportunity to present it.
Playing Our Music - Natalia and I have another hobby that has a special place in our lives, playing music. While we have been playing country music for
many years with dance bands in Ontario, that took
a little hiatus when we moved out of Cobourg, Ontario.
(Continued from page 12)
(Continued on page 14)
Pepper Mill
Pieces Display at Cloverdale Woodshow
AAW Best Newsletter Award 2008

The interest was renewed in the early 2000’s when
we started playing with a group of fellow musicians
in our Square Dance club. That blossomed into the
Cypress Creek Duo where Natalia and I play our
Classic Country and Old Time Rock and Roll music
at retirement residences, care homes, and private
parties. We have a mentor, Nelson Camara, in Mississauga who is a record producer and recording
studio owner. In 2012 we had the privilege to record a 12 song CD at his studio which we offer for
sale at our performances. Recording that CD is an
experience I will never forget.
Where do you display and/or sell your work?
Most of my pieces are on sale at galleries. Some
are on Granville Island, Whistler, and LaConner,
WA. Also, I am currently working with a friend on
upgrading my CusworthWoodturning.com website
to include some dedicated pieces to be sold there.
Who has been the greatest influence on your
work?
I believe that the greatest influence on my
woodturning are the members of the Greater Vancouver and the Fraser Valley Woodturners Guilds.
While I have gleaned a lot of my knowledge from
the people I have met, the demonstrators I have
had the privilege of watching, and the videos I have
seen over the years, I would not have even known
they existed if I had not met the members of our
guilds. Also, I feel it is important that I share what I
have learned with new turners and welcome opportunities to do that wherever they exist. I think
that is called, “paying it forward.”
In summary, woodturners are a special type of
people and most members of each of the two
guilds I belong to are no exception. They share
whatever they know to make the activity a successful, fun, and rewarding hobby. I thank them all for
my experiences and hope I can continue be that
guide for others into the future.
(Continued from page 13)
Turning a Tulip Article
Cypress Creek Duo

Welcome to Linda, as of February 2023, officially
joining the GVWG Board and the WIT (Women In
Turning) Liaison role. Behind the scenes, much activity and idea sharing has been happening and
we’re looking forward to bringing some of the exciting ideas forward and championing them within
the GVWG community.
Health at the Lathe: A Virtual Exchange
Presentation.
Whether new to turning or a seasoned pro, turning
has risks, challenges, and things that can happen
very quickly to cause serious injury or strains.
There are many good resources available, and one
presented by Robin McIntyre, retired health care
worker and part of team of experts who collaborated in the What Aches series in American
Woodturner, is being shared within the WIT Community. We thought many in our club might be interested and benefit from this information too.
The purpose of this segment is to introduce you to
some new ideas or nudge you with important reminders of health issues that you have had on the back burner, and/or maybe to solve some issues surrounding
working comfortably and safely at the lathe. Many of
these practices toward maintaining good health are directly tied to your enjoyment, endurance, and comfort
during turning. All of the jarring, poor posture, inappropriate lathe height, stiff positioning at the lathe, and
white knuckled grip on tools can add up to injuries, fatigue, and decreased enjoyment of your turning experiences.
Please feel free to share this Health at the Lathe video
link with your fellow woodturners.
AAW WIT Celebrating Women’s History
Month
Another interesting nugget shared within the AAW
WIT community and is available for all AAW members to access, is a current feature celebrating
Women’s History Month. Currently the AAW WIT
Community is bring attention to Jean LeGwin who
was honoured with the AAW’s lifetime achievement award in 2018. There simply are so many
wonderful links, archives and resources offered by
both the GVWG and the AAW.
(https://community.woodturner.org/discussion/
womens-history-month-featuring-jeanlegwin#bm1b3f3810-413c-4938-b7055f406f1bf219) Not sure how to best make the link
work.
National Wig Stand Initiative
In follow-up to a member’s suggestion, AAW WIT is
encouraging club members and WIT groups to join
in a national project to turn wig stands, at no expense for the recipients. The goal is to give back to
the community in this worthwhile effort, especially
since cancer has likely impacted each of us, our
family, and/or our friends. Partnering with local/
regional groups who provide free wigs for distribution of the wig stands to get them to recipients in
need while minimizing the expense to WIT members. Some entire AAW clubs have already been
doing this project for some time and we are following in their knowledgeable footsteps. Detailed instructions are available too.
This personal gift to someone who likely needs a
lift during a life crisis is a gift of caring that will truly
be appreciated. Linda and I think this would be a
wonderful skill building/turning activity to do locally and are hopeful that there are other turners
within our community that feel the same. Send a
note to let us know if you’re interested
wit@gvwg.ca .
This is merely but one idea that has come out of
the WIT Liaison meetings that both Linda and I
have been attending. The support, ideas and resources are huge within this community we’re excited to share the possibilities within our local
group too!

Introduction
In planning for this session on chainsaw safety, I
was reminded of the similarities between what we
do as wood turners and what we should be doing
as chainsaw operators when gathering turning
wood.
In 2015, I presented a session similar to this at the
Island Woodturners Guild, in Brentwood Bay.
I am still a member of the Guild, although a long
distance one now.
So, let’s first take a quick glance at wood turning:
•
Each of us have a standard work procedure and
consistent steps that we take whenever working on the lathe. Some of what you use may be
in the following.
•
We carefully and securely mount a block of
wood on the lathe after studying how to get the
best grain orientation out of the turning.
•
We turn it by hand to check for clearance.
•
The tool rest is adjusted to clear the wood and
yet be close enough to support the bowl gouge
properly.
•
We pick up our favourite bowl gouge, one that
we previously had taken to the grinder to touch
up the cutting edge before calling it a day.
•
We had inspected the cutting edges at that
time to ensure we maintained the correct profile on the face and sides of the gouge.
•
We put on our personal protective equipment,
which will vary for each of us. My preference is
to use a zip-up smock and a full-face screen.
•
I have an exhaust fan that is turned on at this

Handling
By Al Landgren
The following article is Part One of a Chainsaw
Safety Seminar delivered in 2023 by Al Lundgren
to the Comox Valley Woodturners Society and is
reprinted with his permission. Part Two: Bar and
Chain Maintenance will appear in the April 2023
newsletter and Part Three: History of the Chain
Saw will appear in the May 2023 newsletter.
Al Lundgren is a major player in initiating safety
guidelines in the timber industry at large, not just
chainsaw safety. For more information about Al
and his role as a health and safety pioneer, check
out this YouTube video by WorkSafeBC.

time and because I use dry wood as a segmented turner, I always wear a good quality dust
mask.
•
At this time, the belt speed is checked and finally after all that, the lathe is switched on and
turning can begin.
Now let’s look at using a chainsaw:
•
Your neighbour gives you a call because he had
a large black walnut felled and the wood is
yours for the taking.
•
You quickly search under the lumber pile, find
your chainsaw, shake off the dust and head
over.
•
So, what is the first thing you do? For many, it
will be to pull on the recoil to start the engine.
•
But, remember how we prepared for wood
turning? The last thing you did in that case was
to start the machine, just as it should be for any
chainsaw cutting.
•
And this is where we start the session.
Safe Chainsaw Handling
Is the wood secure?
•
Just as mounting a block of wood on the lathe,
you must ensure that wood you want to cut
with a chainsaw is well secured.
Don’t do the following to secure the wood:
•
Have a buddy hold the block with his hands.
•
Support it with your feet inches from the running chain. Any of this sound familiar?
•
When we adjust the tool rest to clear the turning, we need to follow a similar rule on the log
we want to cut.
 You need to inspect all sides of the log.
Check the far side for loose chunks, limbs
etc., that can be thrown back at you. Look
under the log for rocks and other loose debris.
 Remember that loose debris, chunks and
limbs can be thrown directly towards your
face if the running chain comes in contact
with any of it.
 And, of course, rocks and other parts of B.C.
can ruin a chain in a heartbeat.
Is the Chain Sharp?
•
Since we know that it is critical to use sharp
tools when turning wood on a lathe, it is just as
important to cut wood with a sharp chain. We
will talk about maintaining the chain and guide
bar shortly.
•
The point is, the saw should have been put
away after use with a sharp chain ready for the
next time. You will do a better job of filing at
the end of the day than when you are in a hurry
to use it the next time.
•
The chainsaws in manufacture today can run
from about 8500 rpm to well over 12,000 rpm.
For that reason, you should never have to push
on the guide bar to make the chain cut.
•
Working with a dull chain is the same as pushing on a dull bowl gouge, only in this case, the
results can be even worse than a simple catch
on the lathe.
Is the saw ready to go?
•
So, if we have a sharp chain and a decent guide
bar, let’s take a quick look at engine maintenance.
•
Find the manual that came with the saw, or go
onto the net, or ask your chainsaw mechanic
and check such things as sparkplug gap, carburetor adjustments etc.
•
Clean the air filter. The simplest and easiest
(Continued from page 17)
(Continued on page 19)

Page
19
thing to do, but oftentimes forgotten until the
motor is gasping for air and your eyes are watering from all the exhaust smoke.
•
Always fill the oil pot with proper chainsaw oil
whenever the fuel mix tank is filled. They are
designed to empty at the same rate.
•
Inspect the little aluminum chain catcher under
the clutch cover. If it is missing, the only thing
that will catch a loose chain will be your knee.
•
Professional saws with full wrap handle bars
have traditionally made use of the handle bars
as a chain catcher.
•
Go over the saw looking for any loose screws
and secure.
•
It can be a pain to have do this maintenance
just when you want to make a few cuts. But remember, if the maintenance had been done
before putting the saw away, it would have
been ready to go.
Are you wearing proper personal protective
equipment?
•
Most people wear running shoes, blue jeans,
tee shirt and a ball cap when running a chain
saw.
•
Remember how you outfit yourself when turning a bowl?
•
Let’s compare the differences between a wearing a regulation hardhat with a protective face
screen and hearing protection, and then compare that to a baseball cap? Whew! That’s a bit
scary.
•
A common location for serious cuts suffered
from a kickback situation is your face and upper
body, most especially when operating a light
weight chainsaw.
•
We will come back to this when we discuss pivot points.
•
You also really need leg protection devices like
chaps to protect your legs in event of a kickback. One of the common locations of serious
injury from chainsaw users is your front left
thigh.
•
Good footwear is a must. Hiking boots are a
vast improvement over running shoes, offering
good traction in various situations.
•
Professional fallers and other chainsaw users in
the forest industry would never operate a
chainsaw without having a pressure bandage
and pocket first aid kit on their person. This a
practice we all need to copy.
•
Chainsaw cuts are never pretty and you need a
pressure bandage to plug the hole.
•
To eliminate situations while working with a
chainsaw, a single bit axe, at least one plastic
bucking wedge, spark plug/bar wrench, screw
driver, round file with handle and a fine - tooth
flat file should be on-hand.
•
Also any other assorted tools like Allen wrenches required for your brand of saw.
•
Have a CSA approved fuel container filled with
correctly mixed fuel. Don’t use a bleach bottle!!
•
Have a container of proper chain oil. The oil is
available at various sources such as Canadian
Tire or any saw shop. OK, a bleach bottle is OK
for the chain oil.
•
If you prefer to wear gloves, use something thin
like glove liners or other light weight gloves.
Heavy leather gloves and/or monkey faced
gloves will impact on your ability to control the
saw in event of a kickback.
•
So, let’s look at what the pro’s do at the end of
each day. The saw went through a visual inspection looking for missing screws, casting cracks
etc. The fuel tank and oil pot were both filled.
The air cleaner cleaned. And since the machine
was to be left on site until the next day, a cover
was placed over the power head. This might be
as simple as the wedge belt, and/or an undercut slab. The point is, when the faller arrived
the next morning, the chainsaw was ready to
work. Not 20 minutes later.
•
It is worth repeating, the pro’s always wear all
the necessary personal protective equipment.
As mentioned, this includes hearing, eye,
hardhat and leg protection devices. It also includes proper footwear. On his person will always be the previously mentioned pressure

bandage and pocket personal first aid kit
Do you have a Plan?
•
Never start cutting up a log without first considering the end-result. Will the log swing towards
you? lift up? Fall down? Or swing away from
you?
•
Remember gravity will be towards the slope of
the hill when bucking a log, not straight down.
•
You need to determine if the cut will bind and
pinch the bar and chain. Conversely, will the log
split open, catching the chain.
•
Determining bind is extremely important to figure before you start cutting. Where is the balance point?
•
This is where the single bit axe and bucking
wedge become handy when the saw gets
pinched. And yes, it happens to the best of the
pros too!
Starting the Chainsaw Safely
•
So, after all that, we can finally start the saw.
•
Some chainsaws have a combination choke/
part throttle/ignition switch. This will allow the
saw to start at part throttle. The designer obviously never worked with chainsaws in the real
world. So how do you safely start a saw, when it
will run at part throttle?
•
All modern chainsaws come equipped with a
chain brake mechanism and this can be helpful.
•
Locking the chain brake when starting a cold
chainsaw will stop any potentially exciting moments with this design flaw. If you decide to try
it, this practise will not harm the chain brake.
•
Most if not all saws have an enlarged pistol grip
designed to allow for your foot to secure the
saw to the ground when starting. This actually
works. Try it.
Chainsaw Control
Since I have been hinting about kick back situations, let’s spend some time on this.
Kickback Zone
•
The kickback zone on any guide bar is at the top
front section the guide bar, right where the
chain starts to rotate down the front. This is the
point where the rakers are no longer protecting
the exposed front of the cutter teeth.
•
If you push the guide bar straight ahead into
the cut, you can almost see the teeth grabbing
more wood than it can cut, resulting in a kickback.
•
This is similar to taking your bowl gouge at 90
degrees and sticking it directly into a spinning
block of wood on the lathe. You can almost see
the gouge flying out of your hands toward the
ceiling. Same thing.
•
I guess it could be said to never touch anything
with the tip of the guide bar in the kickback
zone, but unfortunately, that wouldn’t always
be practical. However, if you can find an alternate method of attaining a clean cut without
boring or coming in contact with limbs, then it
should be considered.
Controlling the Chainsaw
•
Use a proper stance when working with the
saw for good balance. One leg slightly behind
the other.
•
Always, always use two hands on the saw.
•
Maintain a comfortable grip, not too tight, to
allow for reserve strength if a kickback occurs.
Compare it to holding a golf club, baseball bat,
shop broom etc.
Let’s talk about Pivot Points
•
One handed use has the kickback pivot point at
your wrist. The saw will fly out of your grasp
towards your face and upper body.
•
Two handed bent elbow use, has the pivot
point at your elbow and similar consequences
as one-handed use.
•
Straight-arm use, keeps the pivot point at your
shoulder, allowing the saw to fly to the clear
above and behind you.
•
Do keep the saw close to your person for good
control.

•
One thing to consider is that all chainsaws are
designed for right-handed use. The ergonomics
are designed that way, so they balance best
with the right hand on the pistol grip and the
left on the handle bar. All saws are awkward to
use left-handed.
Helpers and Bystanders
Let’s talk about those around you when you
are controlling the chainsaw
•
First of all, it is essential for someone to be with
you whenever operating a chainsaw.
•
If you get cut and need a driver, a young child is
of no use to you in this situation. Always have
an adult with you.
•
Just as in turning, never let them stand in front
of where you are cutting and most importantly
never let them stand directly behind you.
Examples
•
In the late 1970’s a Franklin River log truck driver died when struck in the chest with a flying
tooth when it exploded off a running chain
when he was standing in front of a landing
bucker who was cutting a log.
•
I had a four-inch piece of chain break off and fly
forward when bucking with an 090 Stihl and
never recovered the missing section.
•
A TimberWest landing man was cut from his
hand to his elbow when struck from a flying
chainsaw that kicked out of a cut when he was
standing directly behind the landing bucker.
•
A good friend took his young son out into the
Nitinat Valley on a Saturday, to a location where
he was normally working. He started cutting up
some firewood when he had a kickback, slashing his left leg. He was going into shock as was
his traumatized little boy.
•
Fortunately, he was able to wrap the cut with a
work-shirt and then drive some 20kms back to
get help. This was one hell of a way to learn he
needed both a pressure bandage and another
adult to drive the vehicle when he went out
there.
•
Had he not been able to control the bleeding, it
should be mentioned no one actually knew of
his exact location as he left minimal directions
where he was going and no time when he expected to return. Cell phones hadn’t been invented yet, but even if they had, there is no reception in that location.
A simple rule to follow if anyone enters your
no work zone
Somebody walks in front. Shut down. Somebody
walks behind, shut down. Somebody comes too
close from the side, shut down. Easy….
Some other ideas
•
If purchasing a new chainsaw, buy from a dealer. Canadian Tire and London Drugs are of no
help if you need service work done.
•
The two top brands for the forest industry are
Husqvarna and Stihl. I recommend both for
home use as well. They cost a bit more but will
reliably last for many years.
•
If purchasing another brand, check to see what
the warranty is and make sure it is CSA approved as some are not.
Review
•
Make sure the chain is sharp.
•
Make sure the saw runs well.
•
Wear the correct safety equipment.
•
Have the necessary fuel, oil and tools on hand.
•
Go with a buddy not a kid.
•
Let someone at home know where you are going and when you will return.
•
Don’t start a cut you cannot complete.
•
Remember your pivot points in event of a kickback.

maintenance.
Part Three will be a brief history of the chainsaw.

Safety Guidelines for Woodturning
You mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 31)

March 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page
31
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage.
